segments.text: Imagine your season-end basketball tournament starts next week, and you want to brush up
on the rules.
You upload your league's 200-page rulebook to an AI and ask, how many fouls until I'm
out of the game?
The AI replies with absolute confidence, five fouls and you foul out.
But wait a second, you distinctly remember a game in last year's tournament where a player
picked up five fouls and was allowed to stay on the court.
So you open the document and dig through the text yourself.
You find that the regular season limit is indeed five fouls, but buried near the end,
there is a special section for tournaments, and in those games, players get six.
The AI didn't hallucinate the five foul rule.
It simply pulled the standard limit and completely missed the exception.
The answer wasn't made up, it was just incomplete.
This happens because we tend to assume that handing an AI a file means it reads the entire thing.
The document trap is thinking uploaded means fully read.
An AI can only generate answers based on the specific text that actually reaches its
context window.
A short file might fit into that window perfectly, but a long file forces the system to search
for the parts that seem most relevant and only add those specific passages.
This three-step process manages long documents.
First, split.
The system breaks the long document into smaller pieces.
Next, search.
The AI scans these pieces for keywords matching your question.
Finally, load.
It takes only those selected pieces and puts them into the context window for the AI to use.
This is exactly how the rulebook mistake happens.
The search step successfully finds the regular season foul rule, grabs it, and stops.
It completely skips over the tournament exception, meaning that critical context never reaches the AI.
There is a formal name for this process.
Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG, it is the exact same mechanism AI uses to pull
information from the web or a large database.
The core vulnerability is simple.
When the retrieval step finds the right passages, the AI can answer your question in seconds.
But when retrieval misses a crucial passage, the AI misses it too and gives you an incomplete
answer.
You don't have to passively accept the first answer.
You can actively guide the AI search process to ensure the right passages are found.
This four-move framework improves retrieval accuracy.
First, name the section, using the document's headings to guide the search.
Second, ask one thing, to give retrieval a single target.
Third, share what matters, by pasting the exact passage yourself.
Finally, ask for the quote, to verify the rule.
By applying these precise moves, you force the system to look past the standard rules
and uncover the verified six-fowel tournament exception.
Asking for a quotation isn't blindly trusting the AI.
It generates a specific string of text that you can easily check against the original document.
This retrieval trap is not limited to casual scenarios like a weekend sports league.
The same mechanical error happens when processing apartment leases, employment contracts,
insurance policies and financial aid letters.
These specific types of documents are notorious for burying critical conditions or exceptions
deep in the text.
If the AI's search step misses them, your answer changes entirely.
Uploading a long document and asking an AI for help is a good starting point, but it
should never be your final conclusion.
As these banners highlight, a missing passage can change the answer.
Ask for the passage, then check it.
